title: Is a Heat Pump Really Cheaper to Run Than Gas?
question: Is a heat pump actually cheaper to run than a gas furnace?
alternates: Heat Pump vs Gas Furnace: Who Gets the Lower Bill?
The One Ratio That Decides Whether a Heat Pump Beats Gas
premise: Running cost against gas comes down to one comparison: the heat pump's seasonal efficiency against the electricity-to-gas price ratio times the furnace's efficiency. At 2024 EIA prices a seasonal efficiency of 2.5 beats a 95% furnace in only 11 states, and 30 states need 3 or more. NREL's national model of 550,000 homes finds bills rise in 39% of homes with minimum-efficiency units and 5% with high-efficiency cold-climate units, so most homes save, but among gas-heated homes with AC the share that saves runs from 38% to 99% depending on the equipment, and is lower for gas homes without AC. These are models at 2021-22 prices. Edwards' county model finds 53% clearly save, 19% pay more and 28% show no clear change. The one large measured study is British: replacing gas boilers raised running costs about 190 pounds a year on a flat tariff, while a heat-pump time-of-use tariff saved about 318 pounds; its authors are linked to the supplier, and UK prices are not US prices. Promises of halving the bill fail for gas homes; RMI's US models find time-of-use rates help only with steep tariffs and smart control.
whyWatch: Half the videos promise lower bills and the other half show bills going up, and both can be telling the truth. The national models, state prices and one large measured study show exactly which homes save and which pay more.
tension: Advocates say a heat pump is three times as efficient, so it must be cheaper. Skeptics point out that electricity costs three to four times as much as gas per unit of energy. Both numbers are real, and they nearly cancel.

arc.hook: Two neighbours install the same heat pump. One's winter bill drops; the other's goes up. Neither is lying.
arc.conflict: Efficiency says a heat pump wins by three to one; prices say electricity costs three to four times as much as gas. Which number wins depends on where you live and what you buy.
arc.evidence: The break-even equation with real state prices, then the national models' share of homes that save by equipment tier, then the UK measured study and the tariff effect.
arc.resolution: Most gas homes save with efficient equipment where electricity is not too expensive; a cheap unit in a high-price state costs more to run. Halving the bill is not a realistic promise against gas.
arc.takeaway: Before switching, divide your electricity price by your gas price and compare it with the seasonal efficiency of the unit you are quoted.

questions.question: Is a heat pump actually cheaper to run than a gas furnace?

central.text: Time-of-use or heat-pump electricity tariffs make heat pumps cheaper to run

questions.premise: Running cost against gas comes down to one comparison: the heat pump's seasonal efficiency against the electricity-to-gas price ratio times the furnace's efficiency. At 2024 EIA prices a seasonal efficiency of 2.5 beats a 95% furnace in only 11 states, and 30 states need 3 or more. NREL's national model of 550,000 homes finds bills rise in 39% of homes with minimum-efficiency units and 5% with high-efficiency cold-climate units, so most homes save, but among gas-heated homes with AC the share that saves runs from 38% to 99% depending on the equipment, and is lower for gas homes without AC. These are models at 2021-22 prices. Edwards' county model finds 53% clearly save, 19% pay more and 28% show no clear change. The one large measured study is British: replacing gas boilers raised running costs about 190 pounds a year on a flat tariff, while a heat-pump time-of-use tariff saved about 318 pounds; its authors are linked to the supplier, and UK prices are not US prices. Promises of halving the bill fail for gas homes; RMI's US models find time-of-use rates help only with steep tariffs and smart control.
questions.tension: Advocates say a heat pump is three times as efficient, so it must be cheaper. Skeptics point out that electricity costs three to four times as much as gas per unit of energy. Both numbers are real, and they nearly cancel.
questions.whyWatch: Half the videos promise lower bills and the other half show bills going up, and both can be telling the truth. The national models, state prices and one large measured study show exactly which homes save and which pay more.

arc.hook: Two neighbours install the same heat pump. One's winter bill drops; the other's goes up. Neither is lying.
arc.conflict: Efficiency says a heat pump wins by three to one; prices say electricity costs three to four times as much as gas. Which number wins depends on where you live and what you buy.
arc.evidence: The break-even equation with real state prices, then the national models' share of homes that save by equipment tier, then the UK measured study and the tariff effect.
arc.resolution: Most gas homes save with efficient equipment where electricity is not too expensive; a cheap unit in a high-price state costs more to run. Halving the bill is not a realistic promise against gas.
arc.takeaway: Before switching, divide your electricity price by your gas price and compare it with the seasonal efficiency of the unit you are quoted.

questions.question: Does a heat pump really pay for itself, and does it matter when you buy?

central.text: Payback for a heat pump varies widely with climate, fuel prices and the equipment it replaces

questions.premise: A heat pump does not reliably pay for itself within a few years. Payback should count only what a heat pump costs beyond the system you would buy anyway, and two national models do that, pricing it against like-for-like replacement at the end of the old equipment's life. Even so, NREL's model finds at most 55% of homes with positive unsubsidized lifetime value from any single heat pump option, 59% if every home picked its best option, over 16 years, and Deetjen finds 21% of single-family houses benefit at current costs, a share that small capital-cost cuts would raise sharply. These are models with their own price and discount assumptions; RMI's four-city model at 2018 prices finds most gas homes would not find a heat pump cost-effective, while a Canadian model, with Canadian rebates and a carbon price, finds it the lowest lifetime cost for most households. Payback varies with climate, fuel prices and the equipment replaced. For a gas home, Deetjen finds switching rarely produces a private benefit and almost never in cold climates, and tearing out a working furnace adds the whole installed cost; in the UK, replacing a gas boiler costs a household about 4,121 pounds net over 20 years even after the grant, on a standard tariff. The case changes when the air conditioner also needs replacing: one heat pump replaces both, LBNL finds no cost premium once cooling must be added anyway, and RMI names it the notable exception to gas retrofits costing more, in three of its four cities; the Canadian model always compares full replacements. Minnesota field data put payback under about a year when both furnace and AC needed replacing, 5 to 6 years at a single system failure, and over 10 years, up to 15 to 29, as a pure retrofit; those are small samples against propane and electric resistance heat, not gas.
questions.tension: Sellers promise payback in a few years; lifetime models find most gas-heated homes do not come out ahead at current costs, even buying at replacement time. Both describe real homes, and timing is much of what separates them.
questions.whyWatch: "It pays for itself in a few years" is the most common pitch. The national lifetime-cost models and Minnesota field data show the same heat pump can pay back in about a year or never, and the biggest difference is whether something needed replacing anyway.

arc.hook: "Pays for itself in a few years." Your furnace is 12 years old and works fine. Is that pitch true for you?
arc.conflict: The pitch is one number; the studies show a wide spread, and much of what separates fast payback from never is not the equipment but whether something needed replacing anyway.
arc.evidence: The national models' share of homes with positive lifetime value and the baseline they count against, the gas-home and UK results, then the Minnesota payback with and without a failed furnace or AC.
arc.resolution: For a gas home with working equipment, a heat pump often never pays back on energy alone; bought when the AC, or both furnace and AC, need replacing, the extra cost is small and payback can be quick.
arc.takeaway: Plan the switch now, and buy it when the AC or furnace is due.
